Otolaryngology · published research

Otitis externa

A canine randomized study found earlier clinical improvement with twice-weekly fluorescent gel than with once-weekly gel or conventional care, without between-group differences in bacterial-count reduction. A 22-dog uncontrolled dual-NIR pilot reported improvement after five sessions.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A canine randomized study found earlier clinical improvement with twice-weekly fluorescent gel than with once-weekly gel or conventional care, without between-group differences in bacterial-count reduction. A 22-dog uncontrolled dual-NIR pilot reported improvement after five sessions.

Summary of the Evidence

Two relevant veterinary publications are identified: one randomized study of dogs with otitis externa using a topical chromophore gel activated by light and one prospective single-arm dual-NIR pilot. Neither is a human clinical study. The illuminated gel is a photosensitizing or chromophore system that re-emits light, not a direct test of conventional PBM alone.

Human and clinical evidence

Tambella et al. randomized dogs to weekly light-activated gel, twice-weekly treatment, or conventional care. All groups improved. The twice-weekly group reached clinically relevant improvement earlier or more strongly, but bacterial colony counts did not differ between groups (2020, DOI 10.1186/s12917-020-02311-9, PubMed). Gesuete et al. reported a prospective pilot in 22 dogs treated with dual near-infrared PBM over five sessions. Several clinical measures improved, and no treatment-related adverse effects were reported; the study had no control group, so natural recovery, cleaning, and other care cannot be excluded (2026, DOI 10.3390/ani16152372, PubMed). The database lists 20 dogs for this report, whereas the article reports 22; the primary publication count is used here.

Animal evidence

Both publications involve dogs. No human, laboratory-animal model, or separate mechanistic animal study was identified in these mapped records.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The gel study used a topical chromophore gel with light activation and compared weekly with twice-weekly delivery. The later pilot used dual near-infrared treatment across five visits, including scanning the ear canal and point treatment of the pinna. These protocols are distinct, and the uncontrolled pilot does not identify a best dose or establish whether PBM adds benefit to standard ear care.

Interpretation

Canine reports offer an early clinical signal only. One intervention is a light-activated gel and the other lacks a comparator; no human efficacy evidence is available.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Evidence is limited to two canine publications: a randomized trial of a chromophore-illuminated gel and an uncontrolled dual near-infrared pilot. Both report clinical improvement, but the first did not reduce bacterial counts more than comparison care and the second lacked a control group. Neither supports efficacy in people or conventional PBM alone.
